title: Buy Vietnamese coffee beans online in Australia

image.alt: A kraft coffee pouch in an open shipping carton beside loose coffee beans

sections: Check the blend and format first

A product listing should tell you whether the bag contains whole beans or ground coffee. Whole beans give you room to adjust for a phin, espresso machine or French press. If the label says Culi, it refers to peaberry, the rounded single seed that sometimes forms inside a coffee cherry.
Start with the way you brew

For a phin, use a medium-fine grind and a short pour to keep the coffee strong enough for ice. For a French press, start coarser and use a larger volume of water. If you usually drink espresso with milk, try a small cup first and adjust the dose and extraction to your taste.
Make a 500 g bag work for you

At 18 g per phin, 500 g makes around 27 brews. Keep the bag tightly closed in a cool, dry cupboard and grind only what you’re about to brew. Marking the opening date on the pack helps you judge how quickly you get through it.

title: Vietnamese coffee is more than a drink

image.alt: A metal phin brewing coffee into a glass in a warmly lit café

intro: From the slow drip of a phin to the layers of a Hanoi egg coffee, Vietnamese coffee makes time for the cup.
sections: A brewer that sits on the glass

The phin is a small metal filter with a perforated chamber and a press. It rests directly over a cup as hot water works through the grounds. You can hear the first drops if the room is quiet. That slow pace is part of the pleasure, whether you’re at a café or brewing at the kitchen bench.
Strong coffee meets milk and ice

Cà phê sữa đá brings together concentrated coffee, sweetened condensed milk and ice. Coffee and milk can arrive layered in the glass, with the ice separate or already added. Stirring changes each sip, and the drink lightens as the ice melts. A short brew helps the coffee hold its place.
There’s room for different tastes

In Hanoi, cà phê trứng pairs coffee with a whipped egg topping. In Huế, cà phê muối pairs a strong brew with salted cream. Bạc xỉu takes the cup in a different direction, giving the milk most of the room and using coffee for flavour. Each one is a distinct way to balance the brew.
Try the ritual at home

Put the condensed milk in a heatproof glass, set the phin over it and watch a full brew before changing your recipe. Note the grind and how quickly the coffee drips. Taste it before adding ice. Those few minutes give you a better feel for what to change next time.

title: Why Vietnamese Robusta coffee tastes different

image.alt: Dark roasted coffee beans with a scoop of ground coffee

intro: Understand the body, bitterness and roast behind a strong Vietnamese coffee, then adjust your brew to suit your taste.
sections: Robusta and Arabica in the cup

Robusta often gives coffee a fuller body and a more pronounced bitterness. Arabica can bring brighter acidity and a wider range of fruit or floral notes. Roast and preparation have a big say in both, so origin and species are only part of the picture.
Why it works with condensed milk

The thicker texture and strong roast flavours can still come through after you add sweetened condensed milk. If the coffee disappears after a few minutes over ice, try a shorter extraction volume on your next cup or use larger ice cubes to slow dilution.
How to adjust a phin brew

Start with about 18 g of coffee and 90 mL of hot water. Wet the grounds first with part of the water, then pour the rest. If water barely drips, grind slightly coarser or ease off the press. If the cup tastes weak and the water ran straight through, try a finer grind.
What our label tells you

Hạt Mộc’s Hanoi blend lists Robusta, Culi (peaberry) and Moka. The manufacturer references Đắk Lắk and Lâm Đồng. Start with a short black taste and then add a little milk if you like. That side-by-side taste tells you more about how the blend suits you than judging it only in a sweet drink.

title: Five ways to make Vietnamese coffee at home

image.alt: Three Vietnamese coffees served side by side

intro: Start with one short brew and make cà phê sữa đá, egg coffee, coconut coffee, salt coffee or bạc xỉu.
sections: Start with a concentrated brew

Put 18 g of medium-fine ground coffee in a phin and level it. Set the press on the grounds without compacting them. Add about 20 mL hot water to wet the coffee, wait 30 seconds, then add about 70 mL more. Let the coffee drip through. With an espresso machine, use a double shot as an easy substitute.
Cà phê sữa đá · Vietnamese iced coffee
Brew over 1–2 tablespoons of sweetened condensed milk. Stir until smooth and pour into a glass packed with ice. For iced black coffee, leave the condensed milk out and sweeten to taste.
Cà phê trứng · Hanoi egg coffee
Whisk 2 pasteurised egg yolks with 2 tablespoons of condensed milk until pale and thick, then spoon the foam onto hot coffee. This makes enough topping for two small cups. Serve immediately.
Cà phê cốt dừa · Coconut coffee
Blend 60 mL coconut milk, 1 tablespoon condensed milk and a handful of ice until slushy. Pour the coffee into a chilled glass, spoon the coconut mixture over it and serve straight away.
Cà phê muối · Salt coffee
Whisk 40 mL thickened cream with 1 teaspoon of condensed milk and a small pinch of salt until it thickens but still pours. Pour the cream over hot or iced coffee. Taste before adding any extra salt.
Bạc xỉu · Milk with a splash of coffee
Stir 1 tablespoon condensed milk into 120 mL cold milk. Add ice and top with 20–30 mL of your concentrated coffee. Use the rest for another glass or add it gradually if you prefer a stronger drink.

title: What makes Vietnamese cashews special?

image.alt: Golden roasted cashews with salt on a dark plate

intro: From growing and shelling to the final roast, here’s what shapes the texture and taste of a good cashew.
sections: Growing, shelling and sorting

Bình Phước is a region associated with cashew growing in Vietnam. After harvest, processors remove the shell and sort the kernels. Growing origin and processing location can differ, so check the pack if knowing where the crop was grown matters to you.
What the roast changes

Roasting brings out a deeper nutty aroma and gives the kernel a firmer bite. A good way to compare two bags is to taste them side by side at room temperature. Notice how the toast, sweetness and salt carry through after the first crunch.
Whole kernels and broken pieces

Whole cashews look good in a serving bowl and are easy to eat by hand. Pieces work well in dishes where you’d chop the nuts anyway. A large, whole kernel is appealing but size alone says little about freshness or whether you’ll prefer the roast.
From the pack to the table

Try salted cashews over sliced cucumber with lime or sprinkle them on a noodle salad just before serving. Keep unused nuts sealed and follow the label’s date and storage advice. Hạt Mộc’s cashew packs come from our Hanoi supplier and are already roasted and salted.

title: Where Vietnamese coffee culture thrives in Australia

image.alt: Vietnamese iced coffee and a glass of water on a sunlit café table

intro: Explore the food neighbourhoods where Vietnamese coffee feels at home, from Western Sydney to Melbourne and Brisbane.
sections: Western Sydney · Bankstown and Cabramatta

In Bankstown and Cabramatta, make coffee part of a food outing. Order a bánh mì or sit down for a bowl of phở, then look for cà phê sữa đá on the menu. Canley Vale is another nearby stop if you’re taking the train through the south-west.
Melbourne · Footscray and Richmond

Footscray’s food precinct and Victoria Street in Richmond are good places to explore Vietnamese menus. Look for iced coffee alongside lunch, or ask whether the café brews with a phin if you want to see the slower table-side method.
Brisbane · Inala

Inala is home to a Vietnamese food precinct where you can make a morning of the bakeries, grocers and cafés. If you prefer a less sweet cup, order cà phê đen đá, iced black coffee, and ask about sugar before ordering.
Bring a favourite cup home

Take note of whether you liked the coffee’s roast, sweetness or texture. Start with the iced condensed milk version at home, then adjust the milk or try a glass of bạc xỉu. A small phin and a heatproof glass are enough to get started.
